extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, legislators, and legal practitioners working on separation-of-powers and regulatory design
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly policy-legal guidance about how to structure presidential control, congressional review, and removal rules for administrative agencies—distinguishing executive, legislative, and judicial administrative functions and proposing statutory fixes for enforcement control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional-presentment and assent procedure for rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress takes no action in the allotted time, such inaction shall be construed as assent to the rule, but such rule must still be presented to the President and, before the same shall take effect, shall be approved by him, or being disapproved by him, shall be repassed by two thirds of the Senate and House of Representatives. If any such rule shall not be returned by the President within ten days after it shall have been presented to him, the same shall be a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model language tracks the Rules Enabling Act and Article I, Section 7; an optional one-house veto variant is noted. The presentment/approval timeline and the rule that presidential inaction for ten days makes the rule law are emphasized as simple, politically practicable procedures for permitting rules to become law while preserving executive and congressional roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary presidential authority over executive functions only
rubrics_metrics.description: The President ought to have unitary authority over all of the administrative state—independent commissions as well as executive branch agencies—but over its executive functions only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a middle-ground proposal designed to satisfy both formalists (who demand unitary executive control) and functionalists (who value technocratic independence). The President would not have directive control over non-executive (legislative/judicial) functions of agencies; the proposal preserves independent rulemaking where appropriate while vesting enforcement/control authority in the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of administrative functions (rulemaking legislative; adjudication judicial; enforcement executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemakings regulating private conduct are (at least almost always) legislative and ought to be treated as such. Adjudications that affect common-law rights and liberties are judicial. The other administrative activities are either 'executive' — and thus the President must have control over them — or 'administrative' meaning Congress may structure them as it sees fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article does not attempt to resolve every borderline case but asserts clear categories for the most important activities: treat rulemaking as legislative, adjudication as judicial, and enforcement/prosecution as executive. Other administrative activities fall into the executive/administrative bucket and may be allocated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement/prosecution is executive and requires presidential control
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution—or the enforcement of rules against private citizens—is an executive function over which the President must have ultimate control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the FTC as an example, the critical point for presidential control is the stage where the agency decides to issue a complaint and prosecute. The President should have authority over enforcement priorities and actions in the same way he controls U.S. Attorneys—i.e., the President may order prosecutions or declines and may remove officials for performance of enforcement functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional fix: create removable enforcement commissioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a commissioner who has ultimate responsibility within the commission for enforcement activities under its jurisdiction — a U.S. Attorney–like commissioner who must authorize any enforcement action and be removable by the President while other commissioners remain insulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commissions already have enforcement directors; constitutional administration would require that those officials be directly removable by the President. This can be accomplished by a simple statutory enactment (a few short paragraphs) and avoids the practical and doctrinal difficulties of narrowing for-cause standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative reform: narrow for-cause removal to enforcement-related reasons (impractical)
rubrics_metrics.description: One possible solution is to amend for-cause removal provisions to permit removal based only on enforcement-related reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes this approach but explains it would be up to courts to discern whether a President’s stated reasons for removal are permissible or merely pretextual — a task the Article finds implausible for the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humphrey’s Executor / Myers / Morrison removal-function framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Humphrey's Executor permits Congress to protect commissioners from presidential removal where duties are 'neither political nor executive, but predominantly quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative.' By contrast, Myers applies where an officer performs purely executive functions and the President's plenary removal power governs. Morrison refines the inquiry to whether removal restrictions impede the President's ability to perform constitutional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this doctrinal schema, classification of the office's functions (executive vs. quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial) determines removal rules. Constitutional administration argues enforcement commissioners fall under Myers (executive) while legislative-adjunct commissioners can remain protected under Humphrey's; Morrison's test about impediment to constitutional duty remains relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kagan’s presidential administration interpretive principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When delegations run to executive branch officials, assume Congress intends the President to have directive authority over them; when delegations run to members of independent agencies, assume Congress consciously limited presidential control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kagan’s model uses statutory interpretation as the vehicle for expanding presidential directive authority (including over rulemaking of executive branch agencies) while respecting the statutory structure that creates independent agencies. The Article contrasts this with constitutional administration which rejects presidential directive control over rulemaking but accepts presidential control over enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional review of rulemakings to preserve technocracy and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress would retain the power to review rulemakings under constitutional administration; Congress and the President could mark up and debate rulemakings after the expert agency gives its recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional design aims to enhance technocratic values while providing political accountability — making presidential direction of rulemaking unnecessary for accountability and preserving a role for expert agencies in drafting and recommending rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practice supports presidential directory control over prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical examples (Jefferson ordering district attorneys to cease prosecution under the Alien and Sedition Acts; Washington instructing district attorneys to nol-pros indictments) indicate Presidents exercised directory power over prosecutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article uses historical practice to rebut arguments that prosecution was not considered an executive power at the Founding; vestigial exceptions (e.g., qui tam actions, state enforcement of federal law) do not disprove the rule that prosecution as a federal enforcement function is subject to executive control when wielded by federal officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation-of-powers test: classify offices/functions to determine insulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent commissions are legislative aids and exercise delegated legislative power, Congress can insulate them from presidential control; insofar as commissions exercise executive power (notably enforcement), the President constitutionally controls them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical constitutional test for when Congress may provide insulation (for-cause protection) and when the President must retain plenary authority. It undergirds the proposal to separate enforcement responsibility into removable executive offices within commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed statutory text modeled on U.S. Attorneys to effectuate reform
rubrics_metrics.description: A short statutory provision, based on the statute creating U.S. Attorneys, can effectuate the reform of making enforcement officials removable and responsible for authorizing enforcement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article contends such statutory enactment would be straightforward, doctrinally permissible (consistent with Myers/Morrison/Humphrey distinctions), and would operationalize constitutional administration without wholesale restructuring of the administrative state.
